channel.title: The Dig — HPC-QC integration and resource management
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the HPC-QC integration and resource management preset. Today's ranked reading list leads with 2611.19618 on latency-preserving rewrites and translation validation for dynamic quantum circuits, followed by 2611.17652 on a neutral-atom quantum data processing unit with measured FPGA-to-host NVQLink latency, and then 2611.20222 on a JAX-based GPU-accelerated GRAPE package with feedback; the ordering reflects direct relevance to compilation and scheduling on a small noisy QPU first, HPC-integrated control and QEC decoding second, and adaptable pulse-optimization tooling third. No pay dirt today — 2 to skim.

item.title: Quantum Data Processing Unit for Neutral-Atom Quantum Computers
item.description:
Skim new method — FPGA-based QDPU architecture classifies a 50×50 atom array in 12.5 μs using one matched-filter lane. Eliminating an assumed 150 ms host round trip increases simulated 35×35 target assembly success from 8% to 85% and cuts wall-clock time per assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s.

Grade 0.556 · 3.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Accelerating HPC With Quantum Computing: It Is a Software Challenge Too”

Figure

Target assembly success plotted against added per-cycle host round-trip latency across multiple trap lifetimes, showing severe fidelity degradation when host communications add tens of milliseconds.

Asks

How can classical measurement processing and rearrangement feedback be architected to meet tight real-time latency budgets in scaling neutral-atom quantum processors?

But

Simulated atom-loss model assumes 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom; CNN detector for 104 sites exceeds DSP limits on the target device.

Tools

AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC (xczu49dr on ZCU216) · NVIDIA DGX Spark over 10 GbE NVQLink · Matched-filter and CNN detection pipelines · Quantised GraphMP ranking kernel

Abstract

Quantum computers need real-time classical processing to convert measurement data into feedback within device-specific timing constraints. We introduce the quantum data processing unit (QDPU), an architecture between a quantum device and its controller. Its core is a machine-learned quantum data model (QDM), adapted to the measurement response and noise characteristics of the device. We implement an FPGA pipeline for neutral-atom array assembly that performs occupancy detection and rearrangement scheduling in FPGA logic. One calibrated matched-filter lane classifies a 50×50 array in 12.5 μs. An atom-loss model using a software reference planner evaluates a 35×35 target with a 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom. Removing an assumed 150 ms host round trip raises the predicted assembly success from 8% to 85% and reduces the wall-clock time per successful assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s. A GPU-based outer loop is proposed for refitting model parameters between runs. Its NVQLink transport is measured on the board: over 10 GbE to an NVIDIA DGX Spark, the median FPGA-to-host-to-FPGA round trip is 2.74 μs for 128-byte messages forwarded by a CPU core. A separate 12-bit learned qLDPC kernel is placed and routed for the same FPGA target, with a derived latency of 0.84 ms per round for a [[1122,148]] lifted-product code under code-capacity noise. A quantised GraphMP ranking kernel for the same code runs on the board with a median host-to-FPGA-to-host latency of 50.5 μs with one shot in flight, excluding host-side BP+OSD post-processing. Together, these implementations illustrate a shared architecture with workload-specific models and timing requirements.

item.title: feedback-grape: A JAX-based Python Package for GPU-Accelerated GRAPE with Feedback
item.description:
Skim new method — Presents feedback-grape, an open-source, GPU-accelerated JAX package implementing feedback GRadient Ascent Pulse Engineering with parameterized unitary and measurement gates optimized via recurrent neural networks or lookup tables.

Grade 0.552 · 3.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Integration of Quantum Accelerators with High Performance Computing—A Review of…”

Figure

Schematic of the feedback-GRAPE cycle showing binary measurement outcomes feeding into a recurrent neural network or lookup table to generate next-step control parameters.

Asks

How can feedback-GRAPE be implemented as a general, GPU-accelerated, user-friendly Python package for arbitrary quantum feedback control tasks?

Before

was limited to task-specific scripts for state preparation and GKP quantum error correction (Porotti 2023, Puviani 2024)

But

Restricted to generalized binary measurement outcomes ±1; requires trajectory sampling to evaluate gradient averages.

Tools

JAX · Optax · Flax · Dynamiqs · POVM binary measurements

Abstract

Modern quantum technology applications require accurate control of quantum systems, including a feedback loop in the control process. While open-loop control can be performed using well established gradient methods like GRadient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE), it was until recently unclear how to combine these with feedback from measurements, which are inherently non-differentiable. Recent work has successfully demonstrated how feedback can be incorporated into GRAPE using machine learning, resolving this issue. Following this progress, we have developed an efficient Python package implementing the method of ``feedback GRAPE''. In this hands-on tutorial, we discuss the package in detail based on concrete examples. Built on the GPU-accelerated JAX platform, our package offers a user-friendly interface inspired by the widely-used QuTiP library, including simplified treatment of multi-component systems.
